nameStory: Black oak gets its name from its dark, deeply furrowed bark that's almost charcoal-colored on mature trees. Interestingly, it was once called "yellow oak" because when you scrape away the outer bark, the inner bark reveals a bright yellow layer that was historically used to make yellow dye.
description: Black oak is a large deciduous tree that can grow 50-80 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. It's a member of the red oak group, meaning its leaves have pointed lobes and bristle tips. The tree is easily recognized by its very dark, blocky bark and distinctive leaves that are deeply cut with 5-9 lobes. In fall, the leaves turn yellow, orange, or brown before dropping.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are 4-10 inches long with 5-9 deep lobes that extend more than halfway to the midrib. Each lobe ends in several bristle-tipped points. The leaf surface feels smooth on top but slightly fuzzy underneath, especially along the veins.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is very dark gray to nearly black, deeply furrowed into thick, blocky ridges. Scrape the outer bark and you'll find bright yellow inner bark underneath that stains your fingers.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Acorns are oval-shaped, about 1/2 to 3/4 inch long, sitting in a deep cup that covers about half the nut. The cup has loose, fringed scales around the rim.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are large, egg-shaped, and covered with grayish-white woolly hairs. They feel soft and fuzzy to the touch, unlike the smooth buds of many other oaks.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a large tree with a straight trunk and broad, open crown. Lower branches often droop slightly, giving the tree a distinctive silhouette against the sky.

habitat: Black oak thrives in dry, sandy, or rocky soils and is often found on ridges, slopes, and well-drained uplands throughout New England. It's commonly mixed with other oaks, hickories, and maples in dry oak forests. You'll frequently spot it growing alongside white oak, red oak, and chestnut oak in areas where the soil drains quickly.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late April to May, starting bronze-red before turning green. Small, drooping catkins appear with the new leaves.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with distinctive deeply-lobed leaves that are dark green above and paler below. Acorns begin developing and are green and small.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow, orange, or rusty brown in October. Mature acorns drop in their second year, falling from September through November.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic dark, blocky bark and fuzzy gray-white buds that are key identifying features when leaves are gone.

funFact: Black oak's inner bark contains so much yellow dye that Native Americans and early colonists used it to color clothing and baskets bright yellow - a single tree could provide enough dye to color dozens of garments, making it more valuable than gold to early textile makers!
confusionNotes: Black oak is most often confused with scarlet oak, but black oak has much deeper leaf lobes (extending more than halfway to the midrib) and fuzzy winter buds, while scarlet oak has shallower lobes and smooth, shiny buds. Remember: black oak = deeper cuts, fuzzy buds.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "velutina" means "velvety" and refers to the fuzzy undersides of young leaves and the woolly winter buds. Despite being called "black" oak, its historical name "yellow oak" actually describes a more distinctive feature - that bright yellow inner bark that's unique among New England oaks.
compareHints: Among the red oak group, black oak has the deepest leaf lobes - much deeper than red oak or pin oak. Its fuzzy buds and yellow inner bark set it apart from scarlet oak, while its large size distinguishes it from the smaller bear oak. The dark, blocky bark is more pronounced than northern red oak's smoother, stripe-like bark patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England oaks, white oak is distinguished by its evenly rounded leaf lobes without bristle tips (unlike red oak group species) and its light gray bark.

Among New England's oaks, northern red oak is distinguished by its pointed leaf lobes (white oak has rounded lobes), its large size (much bigger than bear oak or dwarf chinkapin oak), and its relatively shallow acorn caps (deeper than scarlet oak, shallower than pin oak).
Bear oak stands apart from other New England oaks by being consistently shrubby rather than tree-like, even at maturity.
Unlike white oak with its deeply rounded lobes, chestnut oak has scalloped edges with rounded teeth.
Among New England's white oak group, swamp white oak is unique in its preference for wet areas and its distinctive leaf shape with deeper bottom lobes.
Among New England's red oaks, scarlet oak stands out with its deeply dissected leaves that have the most pronounced sinuses (indentations).
Unlike other New England oaks that have lobed leaves (deeply indented edges), dwarf chinkapin oak has simple leaves with rounded teeth like a saw blade.
English oak stands out among New England's oaks by having the leaf and acorn stems completely reversed from most natives - very short leaf stems but very long acorn stems.
Among New England oaks, pin oak stands out for its combination of deeply-cut leaves with sharp points and its distinctive pin-like branching pattern.
Among New England oaks, bur oak is easily distinguished by its enormous acorns with fringed caps and extremely deeply-lobed leaves.
Among New England oaks, post oak is unique for its cross-shaped leaves with rounded lobes and fuzzy undersides.
Unlike most New England oaks, chinkapin oak has toothed rather than lobed leaves, setting it apart immediately from white oak, red oak, and others.
Unlike our native oaks, Turkey oak has those telltale bristly buds and bristle-tipped leaves that you can actually feel.
Sawtooth oak is completely different from all other New England oaks because of its simple, toothed leaves rather than the lobed leaves found on species like white oak, red oak, or black oak.
Among New England oaks, willow oak is unmistakable due to its unlobed, willow-like leaves - all other regional oaks have distinctly lobed or toothed leaves.
Among New England oaks, shingle oak is instantly recognizable by its simple, unlobed leaves - all other common oaks in the region have the typical lobed leaves we associate with oaks.
